message.content: {"passages":[{"reference":"4.1","text":"Leaving Caesarea of Strato, I, Clement, together with Nicetas and Aquila, arrived at Tyre in Phoenicia. At the instruction of Peter, who had sent us, we were received as guests by Berenice, daughter of Justa the Canaanite. She welcomed us most gladly. She exerted herself greatly in the honor she showed me and in her affection for Aquila and Nicetas; in her joy she treated us warmly, speaking freely as though she were an old acquaintance, and hospitably pressed us to care for our bodies. Perceiving, then, that she was allowing us to make a brief postponement, I said, “You do well to hasten to fulfill the duties of love. But fear of our God must be preferred to this. For, since we are engaged in a struggle on behalf of many souls, we are afraid to prefer our own rest to their salvation.”","lexical_decisions":[{"source_quote":"Καισαρείας δὲ τῆς Στράτωνος","chosen":"Leaving Caesarea of Strato","rationale":"The genitive identifies the city historically; “Strato’s Caesarea” or “Caesarea Stratonis” would also be possible."},{"source_quote":"ὡς συνήθης παρρησιαζομένη","chosen":"speaking freely as though she were an old acquaintance","rationale":"συνήθης can describe someone familiar or intimate, while παρρησιαζομένη denotes speaking with freedom or frankness."},{"source_quote":"βραχεῖαν ἡμῖν ὑπέρθεσιν ποιεῖσθαι","chosen":"allowing us to make a brief postponement","rationale":"The object of the postponement is left implicit in Greek, so the English does not specify whether it was their mission, inquiry, or departure."},{"source_quote":"ὁ πρὸς τὸν θεὸν ἡμῶν φόβος","chosen":"fear of our God","rationale":"The placement of ἡμῶν naturally permits attachment to θεόν, yielding “our God”; “our fear toward God” remains grammatically possible."},{"source_quote":"ὑπὲρ πολλῶν ψυχῶν τὸν ἀγῶνα ἔχοντες","chosen":"since we are engaged in a struggle on behalf of many souls","rationale":"ἀγών retains the image of a contest or struggle rather than merely denoting responsibility."}],"source_issues":[]},{"reference":"4.2","text":"“We hear that Simon the magician, after being defeated in the debate at Caesarea with our lord Peter, immediately fled and is committing many evils here. For by reviling Peter with every kind of charge contrary to the truth, he sweeps away the souls of the multitude. Though he is a magician himself, he calls that man a magician; though he is a deceiver himself, he publicly denounces that man as a deceiver. And though he himself came off worse in the debates before everyone and fled, he claims to have won. He repeatedly instructs people not to listen to Peter, supposedly out of concern that they might be bewitched by a formidable magician.”","lexical_decisions":[{"source_quote":"ἐπὶ τῆς ἐν Καισαρείᾳ πρὸς τὸν κύριον ἡμῶν Πέτρον ζητήσεως","chosen":"in the debate at Caesarea with our lord Peter","rationale":"ζήτησις here denotes a formal dispute or debate. κύριος is retained as the honorific “lord” for Peter rather than being treated as a divine title."},{"source_quote":"πᾶσι γὰρ τοῖς ὑπεναντίοις παρὰ τὴν ἀλήθειαν λοιδορῶν τὸν Πέτρον","chosen":"by reviling Peter with every kind of charge contrary to the truth","rationale":"The dative plural τοῖς ὑπεναντίοις is taken as substantivized neuter, referring to hostile allegations or means of abuse. A possible alternative is to take it as masculine recipients: “reviling Peter before all his opponents, contrary to the truth.”"},{"source_quote":"πλάνος","chosen":"deceiver","rationale":"The word can mean a deceiver, impostor, or one who leads others astray; “deceiver” fits the reciprocal accusation here."},{"source_quote":"τὸ ἧττον ἀπενεγκάμενος","chosen":"came off worse","rationale":"This idiom means to emerge as the inferior or defeated party, not literally to carry away something lesser."},{"source_quote":"ὡς δῆθεν κηδόμενος","chosen":"supposedly out of concern","rationale":"δῆθεν marks the stated concern as pretended or merely alleged."},{"source_quote":"ὑπὸ δεινοῦ καταγοητευθῶσιν μάγου","chosen":"might be bewitched by a formidable magician","rationale":"δεινός may mean formidable, terrible, or highly skilled; “formidable” preserves the threatening ability implied by Simon’s warning."}],"source_issues":[]},{"reference":"4.3","text":"“Having learned these things, our lord Peter sent us ahead to investigate what had been reported to him, so that, if matters were so, once we had written he himself might learn; and when he comes, he will expose Simon in the very presence of those before whom Simon had slandered him. Since, then, danger involving many souls lies before us, for this reason we have set aside our bodily rest for a little while and wish to learn truthfully from you, since you live here, whether what we have heard is in fact true. So now please tell us every detail.”","lexical_decisions":[{"source_quote":"προἀπέστειλεν ἡμᾶς ἐξεταστὰς τῶν λεχθέντων αὐτῷ ἐσομένους","chosen":"sent us ahead to investigate what had been reported to him","rationale":"ἐξεταστάς identifies them as investigators or examiners; the English verbalizes that role without adding a separate office."},{"source_quote":"γραψάντων ἡμῶν αὐτὸς μάθοι","chosen":"once we had written he himself might learn","rationale":"The Greek leaves the recipient and contents of the writing implicit, so neither a letter nor a formal report is specified."},{"source_quote":"ἐξελέγξει αὐτὸν","chosen":"he will expose Simon","rationale":"ἐλέγχω can mean expose, convict, or refute. “Expose” accommodates both the personal accusations and the anticipated public confrontation."},{"source_quote":"ἐκείνων ἄντικρυς ἐφ’ ὧν αὐτὸν διέβαλλεν","chosen":"in the very presence of those before whom Simon had slandered him","rationale":"ἐκείνων and ὧν are taken as referring to the people before whom Simon had spoken against Peter. The repeated αὐτόν has different contextual referents, made explicit in English to prevent confusion."},{"source_quote":"τῆς τοῦ σώματος ἡμῶν ἀναπαύσεως πρὸς βραχὺ ἀμελήσαντες","chosen":"we have set aside our bodily rest for a little while","rationale":"ἀμελέω literally means to neglect or disregard; “set aside” expresses the temporary, deliberate forgoing of rest indicated by πρὸς βραχύ."},{"source_quote":"ἀψευδῶς μαθεῖν","chosen":"to learn truthfully","rationale":"The adverb denotes learning without falsehood or deception; “reliably” would be another contextual rendering."}],"source_issues":[]},{"reference":"4.4","text":"Having been called upon, Berenice said, “These matters are as you heard. But listen to the other things concerning Simon himself, which perhaps you do not know. For by making apparitions and phantom-images appear in the middle of the marketplace in broad daylight, he astonishes the whole city. When he goes out, statues move and many shadows go before him, which he himself says are the souls of the dead. Having soon afterward won over to himself many who were trying to expose him as a sorcerer, he sacrificed an ox under the pretext of a banquet and feasted them, then beset them with various diseases and subjected them to demons. And—to keep from saying too much—after harming many, he has been regarded as a god; besides being fearsome, he has also been held in special honor.”","lexical_decisions":[{"source_quote":"ἡ Βερνίκη δὲ ἀξιωθεῖσα","chosen":"Having been called upon, Berenice said","rationale":"Although the passive of ἀξιόω can literally mean “having been deemed worthy,” it can contextually introduce someone who has been requested or invited to speak."},{"source_quote":"φαντάσματά τε γὰρ καὶ ἰνδάλματα","chosen":"apparitions and phantom-images","rationale":"The paired nouns both concern visual manifestations; the differentiated rendering preserves the source’s two terms rather than collapsing them into one."},{"source_quote":"προϊόντος αὐτοῦ","chosen":"When he goes out","rationale":"The participle can describe going out, coming forward, or proceeding in public; the surrounding moving statues and preceding shadows suggest a public appearance or procession."},{"source_quote":"διαλλάξας πρὸς ἑαυτὸν εὐθύστερον","chosen":"Having soon afterward won over to himself","rationale":"διαλλάσσω denotes reconciling or winning people over. εὐθύστερον is taken temporally as indicating prompt succession; it could instead qualify the manner as “more directly” or “more readily.” The supplied reading is retained without emendation."},{"source_quote":"διαφόροις νόσοις περιέβαλεν","chosen":"beset them with various diseases","rationale":"περιβάλλω literally evokes surrounding or enveloping; with diseases as its instrument, “beset” preserves more of that image than the generic “afflicted.”"},{"source_quote":"δαίμοσιν ὑπέβαλεν","chosen":"subjected them to demons","rationale":"ὑποβάλλω here presents the victims as being placed under the power or influence of demons."},{"source_quote":"πρὸς τῷ φοβερὸν εἶναι καὶ προτετίμηται","chosen":"besides being fearsome, he has also been held in special honor","rationale":"φοβερός actively means fear-inspiring, while the perfect προτετίμηται indicates an established state of exceptional esteem or preference."}],"source_issues":[]},{"reference":"4.5","text":"“Therefore I do not think anyone will be able to extinguish so great a fire that has been kindled. For no one doubts what that man claims; rather, each person emphatically maintains that it is so. Therefore, so that you may not be put in danger, I urge you not to attempt anything against him before Peter comes, who alone will be able to contend against so great a power (being the most proven disciple of our Lord Jesus Christ). For I have become so afraid of the man that, if he had not on another occasion also debated with my lord Peter and come off worse, I would have advised you to persuade even Peter himself not to attempt a counter-debate with Simon.”","lexical_decisions":[{"source_quote":"τοσοῦτον ἀναφθὲν πῦρ σβέσαι","chosen":"extinguish so great a fire that has been kindled","rationale":"The attributive participle describes the fire as already kindled; the rendering retains both that existing state and the explicit fire metaphor."},{"source_quote":"περὶ ὧν ἐκεῖνος ἐπαγγέλλεται","chosen":"what that man claims","rationale":"ἐπαγγέλλομαι may mean promise, profess, or claim; here it concerns Simon’s asserted powers and representations."},{"source_quote":"ἀλλὰ τοῦτο οὕτως ἔχειν διαβεβαιοῦται ἕκαστος","chosen":"rather, each person emphatically maintains that it is so","rationale":"With its accusative-and-infinitive complement, διαβεβαιοῦται expresses emphatic affirmation. This preserves a distinction from the preceding οὐδὲ ἐνδοιάζει τις: the people not only do not doubt but positively maintain the claim."},{"source_quote":"πρὸς τοσαύτην δυναστείαν","chosen":"against so great a power","rationale":"δυναστεία can denote power, dominion, or potent authority; “power” best fits Simon’s feared magical capacity in context."},{"source_quote":"τοῦ κυρίου ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦ χριστοῦ δοκιμώτατος ὑπάρχων μαθητής","chosen":"being the most proven disciple of our Lord Jesus Christ","rationale":"δοκιμώτατος is formally superlative and can be comparative, “the most proven disciple,” or elative, “a highly approved” or “well-proven disciple,” without ranking Peter above every other disciple. The main rendering adopts the comparative force because the surrounding clause says that Peter alone can contend with Simon, but the elative reading remains viable."},{"source_quote":"πρὸς τὸν κύριόν μου Πέτρον διαλεχθεὶς τὸ ἧττον ἀπηνέγκατο","chosen":"debated with my lord Peter and came off worse","rationale":"διαλέγομαι denotes discussion or debate here, and τὸ ἧττον ἀπηνέγκατο is the idiom for emerging as the defeated or inferior party. “Lord” is lowercased because κύριος is an honorific for Peter in this clause."},{"source_quote":"μὴ πειρᾶσθαι ἀντεξετάζεσθαι τῷ Σίμωνι","chosen":"not to attempt a counter-debate with Simon","rationale":"ἀντεξετάζομαι denotes engaging in examination or disputation in opposition to another; “counter-debate” preserves that reciprocal adversarial force."}],"source_issues":[]}]}
